Thanks — reporter of #22164 here. Deleting `IngestionTask` / `IngestionTaskLog` rows inside the existing transaction addresses the asymmetry pointed out in the issue (single-document delete cleans them; dataset delete didn't), and keeping RUNNING/STOPPING rows for the owning worker is a defensible rule.

Two questions/notes from the issue side:

1. The kept RUNNING row now references a deleted dataset. Once its pipeline settles (most likely record-not-found → FAILED), what removes that row? If the settlement path's terminal cleanup doesn't cover tasks whose dataset is gone, the orphan window narrows but doesn't fully close. Could the test extend one more step — settle the kept task and assert the row is gone?
2. For awareness, the issue lists two further pieces this PR intentionally leaves out: cancelling in-flight pipelines via the existing `{taskID}-cancel` / `RequestStop` primitive, and dropping the engine chunk table (`deleteDatasetEngineData` only deletes rows). Perfectly fine as separate follow-ups — just flagging so they don't get lost if the issue is closed as fixed.

Good catch, and no: nothing removes that row. I traced the settlement path on current main. When the kept RUNNING task settles, the ingestor only writes the terminal status (`markFailed` / `completeTask` / `markStopped` → `transition`) and the pipeline log; the only code that deletes an `ingestion_task` row is `Remove`/`RemoveMany` (explicit user removal) and `rollbackCreatedTask`. So the row ends up FAILED/COMPLETED/STOPPED and still references the deleted dataset. The orphan window narrows but does not close, as you say, and the PR description already says so.

Because of that I'd rather not extend the test to assert the row disappears after settling: it would not pass without a new behaviour (cancel-and-wait for active tasks before the delete, or a sweep of terminal rows whose dataset is gone), and that is a design call for the maintainers. Happy to do either as a follow-up if you tell us which you prefer; the cancel path would use the existing `RequestStop` primitive, as the issue suggests. Thanks for flagging the engine-table piece too; agreed it should stay tracked separately.

Thanks for tracing the settlement path — that confirms the issue's reading.

Between the two follow-ups our preference is **cancel-and-wait** (option 1): the `{taskID}-cancel` flag is polled every 500 ms, so in-flight OCR/embedding/LLM work for a dataset that no longer exists stops within seconds instead of running to completion; and once the bounded wait completes, the delete transaction can cascade-delete **all** task rows — the "keep RUNNING" exception disappears, and no FAILED row referencing the deleted dataset is ever written. The terminal-row sweep (option 2) is still worth having as an async safety net for rows left by a crash mid-cancel, but as a complement rather than the primary mechanism.

One sequencing note: signal the cancellations **before** the storage-object cleanup starts, so the worker observes the flag while the (slower) object deletion runs — the cleanup window covers the observation latency for free.

Happy to review the follow-up when it lands — and thanks for the `IngestionTaskLog` catch, by the way; the issue missed that table entirely.

Thanks, went with cancel-and-wait as you preferred. Pushed a follow-up commit: before touching storage, `deleteDataset` now calls `RequestStop` on every active ingestion task of the dataset (which sets the `{taskID}-cancel` flag), waits up to 30 s for RUNNING/STOPPING tasks to settle, and if any are still active logs a warning and marks them STOPPED. The delete transaction then removes all task rows and logs of the dataset, so the "keep RUNNING" exception is gone and no FAILED row pointing at the deleted dataset is written. The test now covers a RUNNING task (bounded wait, then removed along with its log); it fails without the stop/wait step.

Looks right, and thanks for wiring the full sequence — the ordering (cancel → bounded wait → storage cleanup → transaction removes all rows) is exactly the shape that keeps the worker from burning model calls for a dataset that no longer exists.

One detail we relied on in our deployment: 30s covers the cancel-flag observation latency (polled every 500ms) many times over, so the timeout should almost never fire in practice; logging + STOPPED on overrun is the sensible backstop. Glad the follow-up carried the issue to completion.
